title: Simon the magician (Acts 8:4–25)
hook: a man who has already believed reaches for his purse. why?
tomorrow: why would a queen's treasurer need help reading?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Stephen's two last prayers, and a young man named Saul standing by the coats. The line: receive my spirit.

A front-row seat, a skip-the-line pass, a bigger following: plenty of things can be bought. Today's story has a man who tries to buy something that can't. After Stephen's death the believers scatter, and Philip, one of the seven, goes down to a city of Samaria. Crowds listen, and "there was great joy in that city." But one man there already has a following: Simon, who had "used sorcery, and bewitched the people of Samaria." Here's the strange part. Simon isn't an enemy. "Then Simon himself believed also: and when he was baptized, he continued with Philip." So why, a few verses later, is a brand-new believer reaching for his money?
screen: `SOME THINGS CAN BE BOUGHT.` → `SIMON, WHO USED SORCERY.` → `SIMON HIMSELF BELIEVED.`

segments.voice: Word reaches Jerusalem, and Peter and John come down. They pray for the new believers and lay hands on them, and they receive the Holy Ghost. Simon watches, and sees what looks to him like a technique. So he brings money: "Give me also this power, that on whomsoever I lay hands, he may receive the Holy Ghost." That's the answer to the puzzle. Simon believed, but he still thought like his old trade: power is something a professional acquires, for a fee. He brought the marketplace into the church with him, without noticing. Peter's reply is fierce: "Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money." The key word is gift. A gift can be received, thanked for, passed along. The moment it's bought, it stops being a gift. Something to tell a friend tonight: it's the same word Peter used at Pentecost, when he promised the crowd, "ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost." Free then, free now. Peter doesn't leave it at a rebuke, though. He tells Simon to repent and pray, "if perhaps the thought of thine heart may be forgiven thee." And Simon's last words in the story are a request: "Pray ye to the Lord for me." Acts never says what became of him.
screen: `IT LOOKS LIKE A TECHNIQUE.` · `GIVE ME ALSO THIS POWER.` · `THE GIFT OF GOD, NOT FOR SALE.` · `PRAY YE TO THE LORD FOR ME.` · then, large: `NOT FOR SALE.`

segments.voice: Count three good things in your life you didn't earn, one finger at a time: a person, a morning, a second chance. With each one, notice any urge to pay it back or prove you deserve it, and set that urge down. Let all three stay gifts, with no price on them.
Simon the magician. A man of Samaria who believed, then tried to buy the power to give the Holy Ghost.
Pocket this one: not for sale, because a gift that's bought stops being a gift. See you tomorrow.
